papers.title: Keeping cats for mummification in ancient Egypt: osteological evidence from Beni Hassan.
papers.abstract: The present study documents a substantial assemblage of cat skulls derived from Ancient Egyptian mummies and housed at the Natural History Museum in Vienna (Austria). Examination of the museum's archival correspondence clarified the collection's provenance and acquisition history during the 1880s. Morphological and osteometric analyses were conducted on 131 well-preserved skulls of small felids from Beni Hassan (Speos Artemidos/Stabl Antar). The assemblage includes a small number of jungle cat skulls (Felis chaus), while the marked size variation among the remaining specimens suggests that, in addition to domestic cats (Felis catus), African wild cats (Felis lybica) and possibly hybrids may also be present. Age-at-death estimates based on dental evidence indicate that the collection is biased towards adult and subadult individuals relative to the age profiles reconstructed from X-ray analyses of wrapped mummies. More than half of the felids exhibit pathologies, primarily dental anomalies, along with healed fractures, puncture marks, and deformations possibly linked to infectious or metabolic disorders. Notably, all but one of the jungle cats show pathological alterations, suggesting that all the felids were housed together and subjected to similar captive conditions. Radiocarbon dating was performed on a subsample of four jungle cats and five other small felids. With the exception of one specimen dated to the Third Intermediate Period, all individuals originate from the end of the Late Period and the beginning of the Ptolemaic era. Stable isotope analysis (δ13C and δ15N) of four Felis chaus and twelve Felis cf. catus reveals dietary or environmental differences, suggesting that the jungle cats likely did not reproduce in captivity.

papers.title: Gender Sensitivity and Sexual Assertiveness as Moderators of the Relationship Between Depression and Cyber Dating Violence Among College Students.
papers.abstract: This study examined the associations of depression with cyber dating violence (CDV) victimization and perpetration among college students, and tested whether gender sensitivity and sexual assertiveness moderated these associations. This cross-sectional, descriptive correlational study analyzed online survey data from 208 university students aged 19 years or older who reported at least one current or previous mutually recognized romantic relationship. Measures were the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale, the Cyber-violence in Adolescent Couples scale, a gender sensitivity scale, and a sexual assertiveness scale. Data were analyzed with IBM SPSS Statistics 23.0 and the PROCESS macro (version 3.2.01) using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, independent t-tests, one-way analysis of variance, and moderated regression analysis. Depression was positively associated with both CDV victimization and CDV perpetration. Gender sensitivity and sexual assertiveness each significantly moderated these associations, with the conditional associations generally attenuated at higher levels of the moderators. Johnson-Neyman analyses identified sample-specific regions of significance rather than universal clinical thresholds. This study indicates that gender sensitivity and sexual assertiveness function as potentially modifiable psychosocial competencies associated with weaker associations between depression and CDV victimization and perpetration. Because the design was cross-sectional, reverse and reciprocal pathways cannot be excluded, and the findings should be interpreted as conditional associations rather than causal effects. These findings suggest that CDV prevention should extend beyond mental health intervention alone and incorporate gender sensitivity and sexual assertiveness components.

papers.title: Clock misalignment, not structural loss, underlies memory impairment following disruption of the mushroom body.
papers.abstract: The Drosophila mushroom body (MB) is a central circuit for many forms of associative learning, including olfactory conditioning, courtship conditioning, and aversive phototaxic suppression (APS). Kenyon cells (KCs), the intrinsic neurons of the MB, can be severely disrupted but not entirely eliminated by hydroxy urea (HU) treatment during development. Here, we show that HU-treated flies are profoundly impaired in short- and long-term memory under baseline conditions and that enhanced sleep restores learning in these animals. We establish the robustness of this finding using multiple behavioral assays and two independent methods to enhance sleep. Mechanistic analyses reveal that HU treatment disrupts circadian clock output, mistiming activity in γ-lobe-projecting dopaminergic neurons (DANs) and MB output neurons (MBONs). We further show that this mistiming is mediated, in part, by pigment-dispersing factor (PDF) signaling onto γ2-projecting DANs. Enhanced sleep restores the proper temporal coordination of these circuits. Strikingly, selectively reducing PDF receptor (Pdfr) signaling in these DANs also restored memory in HU-treated flies despite markedly reduced sleep, demonstrating that correcting mistimed clock signals can reproduce the restorative effects of sleep. These findings indicate that memory impairments after HU treatment can arise from disrupted temporal coordination within the MB circuit and demonstrate that downstream MBON-DAN interactions can support learning when properly regulated.

papers.title: People optimistically search for favorite images.
papers.journal: Journal of experimental psychology. Learning, memory, and cognition
papers.abstract: In many real-world decisions, options appear sequentially, and choosing an option ends the search. These situations are often described as "fiancé problems," since one cannot return to a rejected potential marriage partner if a better option is not found. Mathematically optimal decision makers in such scenarios should use prior knowledge about the distribution of option values, such as their expected value and variability, to decide whether continued search is likely to reveal a better option than the one currently available. Previous work shows that people often sample too few options, relative to optimal benchmarks, when searching through numerical economic values such as prices. Recent computational modeling attributes this undersampling to mis-specified, or biased, prior beliefs, whereby participants expect future options to be lower valued than they should. Here, we tested whether biased prior beliefs might also explain the opposite bias: the tendency to sample too many options in image-based searches, such as choosing the most attractive face. In 10 data sets spanning five image-based choice contexts, we replicated oversampling bias in every data set. We applied computational modeling and, across these image-based tasks, most, but not all, participants were best fit by the biased prior model, which expected future option values to be higher than warranted by optimality. Thus, optimistically and pessimistically biased priors may contribute respectively to over- and undersampling biases. These suboptimal search strategies could manifest in real-world decisions such as shopping, choosing dating partners, or evaluating trustworthy job candidates. papers.title: Exploring the domain of the He-He bond: non-covalent interactions beyond dispersion.
papers.abstract: The structure, stability, and bonding character of a group of helium compounds formulated as He-HeX (X = H+, BeO, BO+, CS2+) were investigated using ab initio calculations up to the coupled cluster level of theory, symmetry adapted perturbation theory (SAPT), and techniques of bonding analysis including the theory of atoms in molecules (AIM), the method based on the graphical representation of the local electron energy density (GLED), and the study of the reduced density gradient. Compared with the purely dispersive He2, the He-He distances and He-He SAPT binding energies of He-HeX are invariably shorter and higher, respectively, and their SAPT binding energies include an appreciable contribution from the induction, which has become, indeed, the prevailing term in the ionic systems. The study of this group of helium compounds furnishes insights into a still little explored domain of the He-He bond, namely the one including non-covalent interactions beyond the mere dispersion.

papers.title: A multi-chain decoupling model of physically cross-linked gels for exploring the poly-N-chain and loop effects.
papers.abstract: Reversible physical crosslinking-including ionic, hydrogen-bonding, and supramolecular interactions-has become a central strategy for toughening gels, yet its topological consequences for polymer network conformation remain poorly understood within classical network theory. Here we propose an ideal thermodynamic multi-chain decoupling framework that quantifies how reversible physical crosslinks alter network topology and mechanical response. The coupled problem is decoupled into two competing contributions: the poly-N-chain effect, in which inter-chain bonding imposes entropy loss and drives end-to-end distance convergence to approximately one-third of the initial chain length; and the intramolecular loop effect, in which cyclization contracts chains and degrades network connectivity. Their competition is captured by a cooperative factor, defined as the ratio of coupled to uncoupled end-to-end distances, which serves as a quantitative measure of coupling strength. Building on conformational entropy and mean end-to-end distance as state variables, we derive closed-form expressions for the strain energy density and Cauchy stress of physically crosslinked networks, extending classical hyperelastic theory to reversible crosslinking. The model is validated against experimental stress-strain data from three distinct systems: polyampholyte hydrogels under varying ionic strength, salting-out PVA gels modified with various acids, and dynamical dual-crosslinked PTMG elastomers. The framework reveals a general design principle: optimal network performance requires maximizing interchain crosslinking probability while suppressing intramolecular cyclization.

papers.title: [Expression of Concern] MicroRNA‑500a‑5p inhibits colorectal cancer cell invasion and epithelial‑mesenchymal transition.
papers.abstract: Following the publication of the above paper, an interested reader has contacted the Editorial Office to raise a couple of concerns regarding the description of experimental details in the paper. First, in the Materials and methods section, it was stated that the miRNA targets were predicted using miRWalk2 and TargetScan; however, in the Discussion section, ZEB1 and ZEB2 were described only as potential target genes identified by bioinformatics, and the authors explicitly stated that further studies would be required to elucidate how miR‑500a‑5p modulates ZEB1 and/or ZEB2. It was not possible to identify an experiment in the main article that directly tested miR‑500a‑5p binding to, or functional dependence on, a candidate target; therefore, the authors should clarify whether a direct target of miR‑500a‑5p was experimentally validated. Secondly, in the Materials and methods section, it was also stated that cells transfected with the miR‑500a‑5p inhibitor were treated with 80 µM emodin for 48 h. A 0‑80 µM emodin dose series for 48 h was also used for the western blot experiments, and Fig. 3E employed a Matrigel assay to conclude that emodin suppresses the increased invasion associated with the miR‑500a‑5p inhibitor; however, it was not possible to identify a matched measurement of cell viability, apoptosis, proliferation, attachment, or viable cell number at 80 µM emodin for 48 h. The authors could have provided the viability and cell‑number data for each experimental condition in Fig. 3, and should clarify whether emodin remained present during the Transwell assay, and also whether equal numbers of viable cells were seeded after treatment. The authors have been contacted by the Editorial Office to offer an explanation for these possible omissions in the presentation of the data in this paper, and we are awaiting their response. papers.title: Immediate Postpartum Mental Health and Sleep in Mothers and Fathers with Healthy Newborns.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The postpartum period represents a critical window for parental psychological adjustment, but whether this is the case immediately after birth remains understudied. Furthermore, while many aspects of maternal mental health have been widely investigated in high-risk contexts, less is known about critical factors such as sleep-related vulnerability and attachment-related processes in low-risk situations, how these relate to early mental health in fathers, or how these factors may be associated with neonatal behavior. METHODS: Thirty-two mother-father-newborn triads, comprising 32 mothers, 32 fathers, and their 32 healthy, full-term newborns, were included in the study. Newborn behavioral functioning was evaluated with the NBAS on Day 2. Mothers completed the EPDS, ECR, and STAI on Day 3. Both parents completed the CES-D, PSS, SCI, and FIRST on Day 3. Correlation, paired-comparison, and exploratory regression analyses were conducted. RESULTS: Clinically relevant elevations on at least one psychological or sleep-related measure were observed in 59.4% of mothers and 28.1% of fathers. Mothers showed significantly higher depressive symptoms, poorer sleep quality, and greater sleep reactivity than fathers. Among mothers, depressive symptoms were associated with greater sleep reactivity, with trait anxiety showing the strongest association with depressive symptoms. Maternal and paternal depressive symptoms were also positively associated across partners. Newborn behavioral functioning was broadly within expected ranges, and no association between parental psychological or sleep-related measures and NBAS cluster scores survived FDR correction. DISCUSSION: Psychological and sleep-related vulnerability was detectable in parents during the immediate postpartum period in this low-risk clinical context, with higher levels observed in mothers. papers.title: Quinoline bridging chlorine-functionalized covalent organic framework for solid-phase microextraction of trace organochlorine pesticides in environmental water.
papers.abstract: Achieving a compromise between adsorption performance and stability remains a critical challenge in the fabrication of functionalized adsorbent materials. In this work, a quinoline bridging chlorine-functionalized covalent organic framework (QCl-COF) was successfully synthesized and employed for the efficient solid-phase microextraction (SPME) enrichment of trace organochlorine pesticides (OCPs) in environmental water samples. The as-prepared QCl-COF exhibited a large specific surface area and excellent thermal and chemical stability. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis indicated that halogen bonding and π-π interactions form between the QCl-COF coating and OCPs, together with the hydrophobicity and large specific surface area of QCl-COF, providing multiple synergistic interactions for the recognition of OCPs. Benefiting from these interactions, the QCl-COF-coated SPME fiber demonstrated exceptional enrichment performance toward OCPs, with enrichment factors ranging from 888 to 4212. Under optimal conditions, the QCl-COF-based SPME was successfully coupled with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and exhibited a broad linear range (0.1-1000 ng L-1), low limits of detection (0.011-0.39 ng L-1), and satisfactory recoveries (78.5 %-119.0 %) for ten OCPs. These results demonstrate that the QCl-COF effectively reconciles enrichment performance and stability, serving as a durable SPME coating for trace OCP analysis in environmental waters.

papers.title: Marital Adjustment and Sexual Quality of Life in Consanguineous Marriages: A Sociocultural Perspective from Married Women in Southeastern Turkey.
papers.abstract: This study examined differences in marital adjustment and sexual quality of life between women in consanguineous marriages (between first cousins) and women in non-consanguineous marriages. Comparing these unions is important because consanguineous marriages are embedded in distinctive kinship, family, and partner-selection structures that may influence women's relational and intimate well-being. However, empirical evidence regarding these outcomes remains limited and inconsistent. The sample consisted of 277 married women recruited from Family Health Centers in southeastern Turkey, including 133 in consanguineous and 144 in non-consanguineous marriages. Data were collected using a sociodemographic questionnaire, the Marital Adjustment Test, and the Sexual Quality of Life-Female scale. Group comparisons, correlation analyses, and moderation analyses were conducted, while controlling for age and number of children. No significant differences were found between consanguineous and non-consanguineous marriages in marital adjustment (p = .26, d = 0.13) or sexual quality of life (p = .98, d = 0.00), suggesting limited practical differences between groups. Higher income and self-selected marriage were positively associated with both outcomes (p ≤ .01), whereas longer marriage duration and a greater number of children showed negative associations (p < .001). Marriage type moderated the association between consanguinity and marital adjustment, but not sexual quality of life. The findings should be interpreted within a sociocultural context in which shared family structures and extended kin involvement may shape relational experiences beyond kinship status. Socioeconomic and relational factors were more consistently associated with marital and sexual well-being. Future longitudinal and cross-cultural studies are needed to clarify these relationships.

papers.title: Adverse Childhood Experiences and Intimate Partner Violence Perpetration Among Transgender and Gender Diverse Adults: The Moderating Effects of Minority-based Factors.
papers.abstract: Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) is a pressing global health concern and is associated with a broad range of adverse outcomes. Emerging work has illustrated that transgender and gender diverse (TGD) individuals experience IPV at disproportionate rates. Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are a robust predictor of IPV perpetration among cisgender populations, yet relatively few studies have examined this relation among TGD populations. Minority stress and resilience factors (i.e., gender-related rejection and community connectedness [CC]) have been linked to IPV. Despite this, there is a paucity of research on the effects of gender-related minority stress and resilience factors on the association between ACEs and IPV perpetration among TGD adults. Thus, the current study aimed to address these gaps by (a) examining the relationship between ACEs and IPV perpetration and (b) investigating the moderating effects of minority stress and resilience factors on this relationship among TGD adults. The current study used data (cross-sectional surveys) from a sample of 137 TGD adults between the ages of 18 and 58. After controlling for age, ACEs were found to be significantly and positively associated with all IPV perpetration types, except sexual IPV, and CC moderated this relationship, such that this association was strengthened at low levels of CC. Gender-related rejection did not moderate the association between ACEs and IPV perpetration. Identification of these risk and protective factors may inform interventions aimed at reducing IPV perpetration amongst TGD individuals.

papers.title: Causal dynamic resonance reduces false positives in detecting causality.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
papers.abstract: Many dynamical systems in nature, such as brains and weather systems, are highly nonlinear and complex. Determining information flow among the components that make up these dynamical systems is challenging. If the components are the result of a common process or become synchronized, causality measures typically fail. We previously introduced Cross-Dynamical Delay Differential Analysis, a nonlinear method for assessing causal influence, along with a complementary approach for dynamical similarity between time series data, Dynamical Ergodicity Delay Differential Analysis. Here, we show that "Causal Dynamic Resonance (CDR)" further improves the false positive rejection rate by adding white noise to the data, without perturbing the underlying dynamical system. This is followed by a study of CDR in coupled Rössler systems, where ground truth interactions are known and in invasive intracranial electroencephalographic data from drug-resistant epilepsy patients undergoing presurgical monitoring.

papers.title: Sexual Violence/Abuse and Cervical Cancer: A Systematic Review of the Relationship.
papers.abstract: Sexual violence/abuse may influence cervical carcinogenesis through increased human papillomavirus exposure, trauma-related immune dysregulation and reduced engagement with prevention and care. However, the evidence on the co-occurrence of cervical cancer and sexual violence/abuse has not been systematically synthesised. MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL Plus, PsycArticles, EMBASE and Scopus were searched for English-language studies published between January 2000 and January 2025. Studies were eligible if they reported the prevalence of cervical cancer among survivors of sexual violence/abuse or vice versa. Risk of bias was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools. Seven studies from community, primary care and gynaecological oncology settings met inclusion criteria, covering a population of 8,840 participants. Among survivors of sexual violence/abuse, cervical cancer prevalence ranged from 5.4% to 32.3% and was consistently 1.5 to 2.7 times higher than among non-exposed comparators within the same settings. Among cervical cancer populations, sexual violence/abuse prevalence ranged from 18.4% to 57.5%, with stronger associations observed for severe or penetrative exposures. Adjusted odds ratios and relative risks ranged from approximately 3.3 to 11.15 at the highest exposure levels, consistent with a dose-response pattern. Findings point to a need for prevention strategies that consider how gender intersects with exposure to sexual violence/abuse. The review also suggests elevated co-occurrence between cervical cancer and sexual violence/abuse relative to global population estimates (~10% intimate-partner violence and ~6% non-partner violence). Limitations include small samples and measurement heterogeneity. Findings support co-produced, survivor-centred and trauma-informed approaches to cervical cancer prevention and oncology care that address barriers to healthcare engagement. papers.title: Screening for Intimate Partner Violence Victimisation in Perinatal Care: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated the prevalence of intimate partner violence (IPV) victimisation identified through routine screening in perinatal care and examined which forms of IPV were assessed by the screening tools used. PsycINFO, Medline, Scopus, CINAHL and Embase databases were searched on 16 May 2025. Studies were included if they were peer-reviewed, published in English, and reported the prevalence of IPV victimisation identified using an IPV screening tool administered as part of routine perinatal care. Risk of bias was assessed using JBI's Critical Appraisal Checklist for Studies Reporting Prevalence Data. Thirteen studies (n = 614,799) were included in a random-effects meta-analysis. The pooled prevalence of any IPV detected through routine screening in perinatal care was 3.6% (95% CI [2.5, 5.1]). Screening tools used across studies varied considerably, and many lacked psychometric validation. Although most tools assessed physical and psychological IPV, psychological IPV was not comprehensively assessed, with limited coverage of domains beyond emotional abuse, such as control, manipulation and isolation. The pooled prevalence identified through routine screening was lower than estimates reported in the broader perinatal IPV literature, suggesting that current screening practices may underestimate IPV victimisation in perinatal care settings. Greater consistency in screening practices and more comprehensive assessment of IPV domains, particularly psychological and sexual IPV, may improve detection in routine care.

papers.title: Mirror comfort and avoidance, contextual support, and illness acceptance after breast cancer surgery: a cross-sectional study among Iranian women.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Breast cancer surgery can alter body image, mirror-viewing experiences, and illness acceptance. This study examined illness acceptance, body image disturbance, mirror comfort and avoidance, and contextual factors among Iranian women after breast cancer surgery, addressing limited quantitative evidence from Middle Eastern settings. METHODS: This cross-sectional correlational study included 103 women after partial or total breast cancer surgery in Kerman, Iran. Participants completed the Acceptance of Illness Scale, Body Image Scale, Mirror Image Comfort and Avoidance Scale, and exploratory contextual items. Spearman's correlations, Kruskal-Wallis tests, and multiple linear regression were used. RESULTS: Illness acceptance was positively associated with mirror comfort (r = 0.452, p < 0.001) and negatively associated with mirror avoidance (r = -0.609, p < 0.001), but not with body image disturbance. In the regression analytic sample (n = 90), mirror avoidance, treatment-related personal/family disruption, and perceived usefulness of adaptation support were independently associated with illness acceptance (R2 = 0.632); mirror avoidance showed the largest standardized association (β = -0.562, p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Mirror-related responses may provide rehabilitation-relevant information beyond general body image. Interdisciplinary, preference-sensitive preparation, and supported mirror-assisted self-care warrant evaluation in prospective and interventional studies.
